sources.text:
# C07E11 - research notes

The fixture is `accounts(id, name, balance)` populated with two rows
of 100. The transfer transaction reads the starting balances, debits
30 from one account, credits 30 to the other, and asserts the final
state is `[70, 130]`. The forced-rollback case throws an error inside
the transaction; the engine discards the temporary write pair and the
final state is `[100, 100]`.

The PGlite transaction API is a callback-based promise that commits
on resolve and rolls back on throw. The lesson uses the API, not
`BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` raw SQL, because the in-process PGlite
boundary treats those as session-level operations on a single
connection. The atomicity observation is a
`PGLITE_TRANSACTION_SEMANTICS` claim and a
`RELATIONAL_SQL_SEMANTICS` claim about the visible SQL.

The lesson is explicit that this is single-process atomicity. It does
not establish isolation between two real concurrent sessions, lock
contention, deadlock detection, or recovery from server failure. Those
are separate lessons.

reference notes; no SQL execution is claimed for this sample run. Review only against the supplied material. Do not infer that this sample was executed now or that its references establish general educational accuracy.

findings.title: Forced rollback final state misstated
findings.explanation: Narration claims balances remain [70, 130] after forced rollback, while lesson-source states the forced-rollback final state is [100, 100] and reserves [70, 130] for the committed transfer.
findings.suggestedChange: Correct narration to state committed transfer ends at [70, 130] and forced rollback restores [100, 100].

findings.title: Isolation between concurrent sessions overstated
findings.explanation: Narration claims the experiment proves isolation between two real concurrent synchronized sessions, while lesson-source explicitly says it does not establish isolation between two real concurrent sessions and is single-process atomicity only.
findings.suggestedChange: Remove concurrent-session isolation claim and state the lesson shows single-process atomicity only, not isolation, lock contention, deadlock, or recovery.
